lead: A stereoscopic display sends a slightly different image to each eye. The brain compares the two and reads the difference as depth. A single flat screen cannot do this alone, so every stereo display is really two displays — two images, two optical paths or two time slots — arranged so the left eye sees only the left image. Cinema, VR headsets and 3D monitors all use this trick. This chapter gives the geometry that decides where a point appears, then the main technologies and the limits that decide whether the result is comfortable.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 on binocular depth cues, and Chapter 3.3 on display families.

sections.h3: Disparity decides where each point appears

blocks.text: The two eyes sit about e = 63 mm apart. Look at a point at distance Z through a screen at distance D. That point lands at two different places on the screen, one as seen by each eye. The gap between those places is the disparity, and the brain turns it into depth.

blocks.where: s = signed separation of the two images measured on the screen, in mm, positive when the point appears in front of the screen; e = interocular distance, about 63 mm for an adult; D = distance from the eyes to the screen, in mm; Z = distance from the eyes to the point being shown, in mm.

blocks.text: Read the sign. If Z < D, the disparity is crossed: the left eye's copy sits to the right of the right eye's copy, so the eyes converge in front of the screen and the point appears in front of the glass. If Z > D, s is negative, the images are uncrossed, and the point sits behind the screen. Z = D gives s = 0 and the point sits on the glass. That is the zero disparity plane; a stereo scene is built by choosing a screen plane and pushing objects to either side of it.
Numbers: e = 63 mm, D = 500 mm, Z = 400 mm. Then s = 63 × (500/400 − 1) = 63 × 0.25 = 15.75 mm, positive, so the point floats 100 mm in front of the screen.

The eyes focus on the screen at D but converge on the point at Z. That mismatch is vergence–accommodation conflict, the main source of stereo eye strain. Keep disparity small: a common comfort guideline is about 1° of visual angle, which at D = 500 mm is 500 tan 1° ≈ 8.7 mm of separation. Large crossed disparity hurts more than large uncrossed, because near objects demand more convergence.

sections.h3: Time multiplexing: one panel, two frames

blocks.text: An active shutter system uses one panel and shows frames in turn: left, right, left, right. Liquid-crystal glasses darken the eye that should not see the current frame. Panel and glasses must agree on which frame is which, so an emitter on the display sends an infrared pulse before each frame; some systems use a cable instead.

blocks.where: f_eye = frames per second reaching each eye; f_panel = panel refresh rate in Hz, counting both eyes' frames; t = duration of one slot in milliseconds.

blocks.text: The figure is a 120 Hz panel. Each slot lasts 1/120 s = 8.3 ms. The left image is on screen during slot L1 and only the left shutter is open; then R1 with the right shutter open. Each eye therefore receives 60 frames per second, and one eye's frames are 16.7 ms apart.

Drop the panel to 60 Hz and each eye gets 30 frames per second — visible flicker — and every slot is 16.7 ms long, so the wrong image stays on screen longer. That is why shutter systems ask for at least 100–120 Hz. Pixel response time must also fit inside the slot, or the tail of the left image is still glowing when the right shutter opens.

That leak is crosstalk, also called ghosting: the fraction of one eye's image that reaches the other eye, quoted as a percentage. Under about 1% looks clean; a few percent shows as a double edge on high-contrast objects and adds strain.

sections.h3: Colour, polarisation and space instead of time

items: Anaglyph. The two images are printed in complementary colours, usually red and cyan, and seen through matching filters; the red filter passes the red image and blocks the cyan one. Cheap on paper and on any screen, but colour is destroyed.
Linear polarisation. Two images are shown through polarising filters at 90° to each other and the glasses carry the matching pair. Separation collapses if the viewer tilts their head.
Circular polarisation. Same idea with left- and right-handed circular filters, which survive head tilt. Cinemas use it, with a silvered screen that keeps polarisation intact.
Lenticular. A sheet of cylindrical lenses in front of the panel sends even pixel columns to one eye and odd columns to the other, so no glasses are needed.
Parallax barrier. A grid of thin slits does the same job by blocking light instead of bending it; it costs brightness as well as resolution.

Head-mounted display. Two small panels, one per eye, with fixed lenses. Disparity is exact and crosstalk depends on the panels and optics, not on the room; the cost is weight and a per-user interpupillary distance setting.

blocks.text: The lens and barrier methods are autostereoscopic: no glasses, but each eye sees only half the pixels, so horizontal resolution halves, and the viewer must stay in a narrow band of positions — the sweet spots — or the eyes swap and depth inverts.

examples.question: A shutter-glasses stereo display runs its panel at 120 Hz. (a) How many frames per second does each eye receive? (b) How long is each slot, and how far apart are two frames for the same eye? (c) The panel is switched to 60 Hz. Repeat (a) and (b) and state what the viewer notices.
steps: Panel refresh f_panel = 120 Hz, so the panel shows 120 frame slots every second, alternating left and right.
Each eye gets half of them: f_eye = 120/2 = 60 frames per second.
One slot lasts t = 1/120 s = 0.008333 s = 8.33 ms.
Consecutive frames for the same eye have the other eye's slot between them, so the interval is 2 × 8.33 = 16.67 ms, which is 1/60 s.
At 60 Hz: f_eye = 60/2 = 30 frames per second, and one slot lasts 1/60 s = 16.67 ms.
30 frames per second per eye flickers visibly, and the longer 16.7 ms slot lets more of the wrong image leak through the shutter. Shutter systems therefore need a panel of at least 100–120 Hz.
examples.answer: Each eye receives 60 frames per second at 120 Hz (8.33 ms slots, 16.67 ms apart), and 30 frames per second at 60 Hz, which flickers visibly.

traps: Swapping crossed and uncrossed disparity, which puts near objects behind the screen and far ones in front. Check the sign of D/Z − 1 before drawing the scene.
Reporting the panel refresh rate as the per-eye rate. A 120 Hz shutter panel gives 60 frames per eye, not 120.
Forgetting that s scales with e and D. The same object distance gives a different disparity on a phone held at 300 mm and on a cinema screen seen from 10 m.
Treating ghosting as a cosmetic flaw. Crosstalk of a few percent is an exam-worthy limit: it breaks fusion on high-contrast edges and adds strain.
Assuming zero disparity means no depth. It only fixes the screen plane; all other depths are measured from it.

quiz.q: What is crossed disparity, and what depth does it produce?
quiz.a: The left eye's image lies to the right of the right eye's image, so the eyes converge in front of the screen; the point appears in front of the screen surface.

quiz.q: Why does an anaglyph display damage colour?
quiz.a: Each eye sees the scene through a filter that passes one band and blocks the other, so each eye receives only part of the spectrum. The brain fuses the two partial-colour views and the mixed colours are wrong.

quiz.q: A point is shown at Z = 450 mm on a screen at D = 600 mm, with e = 63 mm. Find s and state where the point appears.
quiz.a: D/Z = 600/450 = 1.3333. s = 63 × (1.3333 − 1) = 63 × 0.3333 = 21.0 mm. Positive, so the images are crossed and the point appears 150 mm in front of the screen.

quiz.q: A shutter panel refreshes at 144 Hz. Give the per-eye frame rate and the slot length.
quiz.a: f_eye = 144/2 = 72 frames per second per eye. Slot t = 1000/144 = 6.94 ms.

quiz.q: Why must shutter glasses be synchronised to the display, and what does the viewer see if the link fails?
quiz.a: The glasses must blank the eye whose frame is not on screen. If the link is lost or drifts, one or both eyes see both frames, giving ghosting; if the pattern inverts, each eye gets the other eye's image and depth reverses, a pseudoscopic effect that is confusing and painful to view.

quiz.q: Compare an autostereoscopic lenticular display with a shutter display for a museum kiosk.
quiz.a: Lenticular needs no glasses, which suits walk-up public use, but it halves horizontal resolution and works only inside narrow sweet spots, so the visitor must stand in the right place. Shutter keeps full resolution and a wide viewing zone but needs glasses, IR synchronisation and a panel of 100–120 Hz, plus battery and hygiene management for shared glasses.

quiz.q: Define crosstalk in a stereo display.
quiz.a: The fraction of one eye's image that leaks into the other eye, quoted as a percentage; it appears as a faint double image on high-contrast edges.

beyond: Not for the exam. Comfortable stereo is now limited less by the optics than by the fixed focus of the screen, so research moves to varifocal and multifocal displays that steer focus with the rendered depth. Light-field and holographic displays try to reproduce the whole wavefront, removing glasses and the sweet-spot problem at once. Retinal scanning displays bypass the panel entirely. In industry, stereo pairs are shipped inside standard formats and engines, so the practical skill is reading disparity budgets and crosstalk figures from a datasheet. Search for vergence–accommodation conflict, light-field display, varifocal display and stereoscopic disparity budget to go further.
